newsitem.title: CHILE: Rain-drenched Chile ends drought measures.
newsitem.headline: Rain-drenched Chile ends drought measures.

text.p: A drought that had dried up reservoirs and shriveled fruit crops in central Chile came to a symbolic end on Monday when the government lifted strict electricity conservation measures after torrential rains.
Energy Minister Alejandro Jadresic acknowledged the dry spell was practically over by ending a reduction in hydroelectric output and consumption limits on industry, imposed in April.
"As of today, we are eliminating the reduction in voltage. The steps taken to save electricity are being relaxed," Jadresic told a news conference.

The rains returned in time to avert full-scale power rationing, which otherwise would probably have started this month, officials said. Water companies have stopped television and radio advertisements urging Chileans to save water.
With little fossil fuel of its own, Chile relies on hydroelectric power for about 65 percent of its energy consumption.

Of the three main reservoirs supplying power to Santiago, two are now at or above normal levels, officials said. The yearlong drought had reduced all three to little more than puddles, worsened Santiago's notorious air pollution and hurt the quality of fruit crops, one of Chile's top exports.
Heavy rains since mid-May, especially in the past week, have caused localised flooding and mudslides north of Santiago, while heavy snows cut border passes over the Andes to Argentina.
At least six deaths have been attributed to the rains. Five army conscripts were killed last Thursday when a flash flood overturned their jeep near the northern town of Copiapo.

The water shortage also drastically cut share prices for the country's hydroelectric companies, including Endesa and Colbun, by forcing them to cut the amount of electricity generated at their dams or buy fossil fuels on the spot market to maintain output.
